subject: Science
board: National Curriculum KS3 (aligned to AQA GCSE progression)
source: Drive: Schemes of work Science 'Science - Y8_9 - Autumn 2 - Termly Plan' (nutrition and digestion, atoms/elements/compounds/mixtures, resources, carbon cycle and climate), 'science KS3 SOW', Biology/Chemistry/Physics 5yr SoW; National Curriculum KS3 Science

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, proteins and lipids
objectives: Name the three main nutrients that provide energy and building materials
State the function and food sources of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids
Describe the tests for starch, glucose, protein and fat

keywords.def: a substance in food that the body needs
a nutrient that provides energy, such as starch and sugar
a nutrient used for growth and repair
a fat or oil that stores energy and insulates

starter: Bismillah. Name the seven things a balanced diet needs.
Why do we need food?
Which foods do you think contain a lot of starch?

teach.heading: What is in food?
bullets: Seven groups: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water
teach.note: Ask pupils to read a food label and spot nutrients. Allah has provided pure and good food: link to Qur'an 2:168, eat of what is lawful and good (halal and tayyib).

teach.heading: Carbohydrates
teach.note: Carbohydrates are made of sugar units. Starch is a large molecule made of many glucose units. Misconception: all carbohydrates are sugary.

teach.heading: Proteins
bullets: Sources: meat, fish, eggs, beans, lentils
teach.note: Muscle repair and growth, making enzymes. About 20 amino acids. Include vegetarian sources such as lentils, chickpeas, tofu.

teach.heading: Lipids
bullets: More energy per gram than carbohydrates
teach.note: Fat provides about 37 kJ per gram, carbohydrates and protein about 17 kJ per gram. We need some fat; too much can harm health.

teach.heading: Food tests
bullets: Protein: biuret turns purple; fat: brown paper
teach.note: Practical demonstration safe online: iodine, Benedict's and biuret reagents are not household chemicals, so show a video of the tests. The brown paper test for fat can be done at home: rub butter or oil on brown paper or kitchen paper; a see-through spot appears.

practice: Which nutrient provides most of our immediate energy?
What colour does iodine turn in the presence of starch?
Name two good sources of protein.
independent: Make a table of the three nutrients: function, food sources and food test.
Carry out the brown paper test on three foods and record the results.
Explain why athletes eat more carbohydrates before a race.
exit: What is the function of protein?
What test would you use for starch?
lessons.homework: Analyse the label of one packaged food and list how many grams of carbohydrate, protein and fat it contains.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a food sorting activity with pictures. Stretch: explain why fats provide more energy per gram than carbohydrates.

lessons.title: Atoms and elements
objectives: Define an atom and an element
Use chemical symbols for common elements
Describe the difference between atoms and molecules

keywords.def: the smallest particle of an element
a substance made of only one type of atom
one or two letters used to represent an element
two or more atoms joined together

starter: Bismillah. What are the three states of matter?
What do you think everything is made of?
What does 'pure' mean?

teach.heading: Atoms
bullets: All matter is made of atoms
teach.note: Atoms are so small that millions fit across the full stop at the end of this sentence. Ancient Greek thinkers like Democritus proposed atoms; Dalton developed the idea in 1803.

teach.heading: Elements
bullets: An element has one type of atom
Each has a name and symbol
teach.note: Examples: oxygen, carbon, iron, gold. Around 90 occur naturally. The rest are made in laboratories.

teach.heading: Symbols
bullets: Some come from Latin: Na, Fe, K
teach.note: Na for sodium (natrium), Fe for iron (ferrum), K for potassium (kalium), Cu for copper, Au for gold. Common error: writing CO for Co (cobalt vs carbon monoxide); introduce briefly.

teach.heading: Molecules
teach.note: Oxygen exists as O₂ (two atoms). Misconception: all elements are single atoms. Many non-metals form molecules.

teach.heading: Arabic roots in chemistry
bullets: Words like alkali and alcohol come from Arabic
teach.note: Jabir ibn Hayyan is credited with early laboratory methods. Keep claims modest. Alkali (al-qili) and alcohol (al-kuhl) have Arabic origins. Link: Muslim scholars helped develop early chemistry.

practice: What is the symbol for sodium? For iron?
Is water an element? Explain.
How many atoms are in one molecule of oxygen, O₂?
independent: Make flashcards of 15 elements with their name and symbol.
Draw a particle diagram showing an element, and a diagram showing a molecule of oxygen.
Write a paragraph explaining the difference between an atom and an element.
exit: Define element.
What is the symbol for gold?
lessons.homework: Learn the symbols for the first 20 elements and write them from memory.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide symbol cards with pictures. Stretch: research why some symbols come from Latin names.

lessons.title: Earth's resources and recycling
objectives: Describe the Earth as the source of almost all our resources
Distinguish between renewable and finite resources
Explain why recycling is important

keywords.def: a useful material or source of energy from the Earth
will eventually run out
can be replaced as fast as it is used
processing used materials to make new products

starter: Bismillah. Name three things in your home that came from the Earth.
What do we do with an empty plastic bottle?
What does 'waste' mean?

teach.heading: Resources from the Earth
teach.note: Sort household items by origin. Almost everything comes from the Earth, from the Sun's energy or from living things.

teach.heading: Finite and renewable
teach.note: Fossil fuels took millions of years to form. Misconception: renewable means unlimited; wood is renewable only if trees are replanted.

teach.heading: Recycling
teach.note: Recycling aluminium uses about 5% of the energy needed to make it from ore (accurate figure often quoted around 95% saving). Say 'far less energy'.

teach.heading: Stewardship
bullets: Allah made the Earth for us
We are trusted to look after it
teach.note: Qur'an 7:31 says Allah does not love those who waste. Discuss practical reuse and sadaqah (donate old items).

teach.heading: Reduce, reuse, recycle
teach.note: Safe activity: a home audit of what is recycled. Look at recycling symbols on packaging. Do not handle broken glass or sharp cans.

practice: Give two examples of finite resources.
Why is wood only renewable if we replant trees?
Name two materials that can be recycled.
independent: Sort 12 items into finite or renewable resources.
Make a poster to persuade people to recycle, with three scientific reasons.
Explain how recycling helps to reduce waste and energy use.
exit: What does finite mean?
State one benefit of recycling.
lessons.homework: Do a household recycling audit for one day and record what was recycled and what was thrown away.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide picture sorting cards. Stretch: evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of recycling plastics.

lessons.title: Vitamins, minerals, fibre and water
objectives: State the function of vitamins, minerals, fibre and water
Link deficiencies to health problems
Plan meals which contain all nutrient groups

keywords.def: a nutrient needed in small amounts to stay healthy
a nutrient such as calcium or iron needed in small amounts
plant material we cannot digest, which keeps food moving
a lack of a nutrient, which causes illness

starter: Bismillah. State the function of carbohydrates and proteins.
Which test shows starch?
Why is water important?

teach.heading: Vitamins
teach.note: Lack of vitamin C causes scurvy; lack of vitamin D causes rickets. Vitamin D can be made in skin with sunlight. Mention that many in the UK need supplements in winter (NHS advice).

teach.heading: Minerals
bullets: Sources: milk, green vegetables, red meat
teach.note: Lack of iron causes anaemia. Include vegetarian sources such as spinach and lentils. Calcium also for muscles and nerves.

teach.heading: Fibre
teach.note: Sources: wholegrain bread, vegetables, fruit. Misconception: fibre gives energy; it does not because we cannot digest it.

teach.heading: Water
teach.note: Link to Qur'an 21:30: Allah made every living thing from water. Fluids are lost by sweating and breathing. The recommended intake is around 6 to 8 glasses a day.

teach.heading: Fasting and health
teach.note: Briefly note that Muslim children do not fast until the age of puberty, and the sunnah encourages dates and water to break the fast. Keep this positive and sensitive; no pressure to share personal practice.

practice: Which mineral is needed for strong bones?
What deficiency disease is caused by lack of vitamin C?
Why do we need fibre if we cannot digest it?
independent: Complete a table of vitamin or mineral, function, source and deficiency disease.
Plan a day of meals and highlight where each nutrient group appears.
Write a short paragraph explaining why water is vital for the body.
exit: Name a disease caused by a nutrient deficiency.
What is the function of fibre?
lessons.homework: Make a healthy eating leaflet for younger pupils on vitamins and minerals.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a matching exercise with pictures. Stretch: explain why too much of some vitamins can be harmful.

lessons.title: The Periodic Table
objectives: Describe how the Periodic Table is organised
Locate metals and non-metals
Use groups to predict properties and patterns

keywords.def: a chart of all the elements arranged by atomic number
a vertical column of elements with similar properties
a horizontal row of elements
a shiny element that conducts heat and electricity

starter: Bismillah. What is an element?
Give the symbols for carbon, oxygen, sodium and iron.
What is a metal? Give three properties.

teach.heading: Organising elements
bullets: He left gaps for undiscovered elements
Elements are arranged by atomic number
teach.note: Mendeleev predicted properties of elements that had not yet been discovered, such as gallium (eka-aluminium) and germanium. Evidence supports the model. Link to scientific prediction.

teach.heading: Groups and periods
bullets: Elements in a group react similarly
teach.note: Group 1 (alkali metals), Group 7 (halogens), Group 0 (noble gases). Use a coloured chart. Ask: which group is lithium in?

teach.heading: Metals and non-metals
teach.note: Most elements are metals. Properties of metals: shiny, malleable, ductile, good conductors. Non-metals: dull, brittle, poor conductors. Hydrogen is a non-metal placed top left.

teach.heading: Group 1: alkali metals
teach.note: Practical demonstration safe online: show a teacher video of lithium, sodium and potassium in water. Pupils should never attempt this at home. Emphasise safety in a lab (goggles, small pieces, safety screen).

teach.heading: Group 0: noble gases
teach.note: Helium in balloons; argon in light bulbs; neon in signs. Unreactive because they have full outer shells (GCSE link; do not push detail).

practice: In which group is sodium?
Is chlorine a metal or non-metal?
Why did Mendeleev leave gaps?
independent: Colour a blank Periodic Table to show metals, non-metals, and groups 0, 1 and 7.
Complete a table of properties of metals and non-metals.
Predict how potassium reacts with water compared with lithium, and explain.
exit: What is a group in the Periodic Table?
Name one property of metals.
lessons.homework: Research one element and make a fact file with symbol, group, properties and uses.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a colour-coded periodic table. Stretch: explain why elements in the same group react similarly.

lessons.title: A balanced diet and food tests
objectives: Explain what is meant by a balanced diet
Use data to compare energy content of foods
Explain the effects of an unbalanced diet

keywords.def: a diet with the right amounts of all nutrients
a condition caused by an unbalanced diet
being very overweight, which can harm health
a unit of energy

starter: Bismillah. Name the seven nutrients.
Which nutrient group is deficient in scurvy?
What is in your typical lunch?

teach.heading: Balanced diet
bullets: Enough energy but not too much
teach.note: Different people need different diets (age, activity, health). Discuss the Eatwell guide proportions: about a third fruit and vegetables, a third starchy foods.

teach.heading: Unbalanced diets
teach.note: Handle sensitively. Avoid body shaming. Obesity increases risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Malnutrition includes both too little and too much.

teach.heading: Energy in food
bullets: Food labels give energy per 100 g
teach.note: Give a table: 100 g of oil about 3700 kJ, 100 g of rice cooked about 570 kJ, 100 g of apple about 200 kJ (approximate). Pupils compare data to explain differences.

teach.heading: Practical: calorimetry
teach.note: Safe online approach: show a teacher video of burning a crisp or nut under a boiling tube of water. This must not be done at home. Pupils use the data (temperature rise) to calculate energy.

teach.heading: Eating well and thankfully
teach.note: Qur'an 7:31 on eating without excess. Mention the importance of sharing food with neighbours and those in need.

practice: Which has more energy per 100 g: oil or apple?
Name one health problem caused by eating too much sugar.
Why do athletes need more energy?
independent: Plan a balanced menu for one day for a teenager and identify the nutrients in each meal.
Use the data to rank five foods by energy per 100 g and explain the pattern.
Write a short paragraph about the consequences of an unbalanced diet.
exit: What is a balanced diet?
Give one effect of eating too little.
lessons.homework: Keep a food diary for one day and identify which nutrients each meal provided.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a planning template and a word bank. Stretch: calculate the energy in a portion from a food label.

lessons.title: The carbon cycle
objectives: Describe how carbon moves between the atmosphere, plants, animals and fossil fuels
Name the processes that add and remove carbon dioxide from the air
Draw and explain a carbon cycle

keywords.def: the movement of carbon between living things, air, oceans and rocks
the process plants use to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light
burning a fuel in oxygen
a fuel formed over millions of years from dead organisms

starter: Bismillah. Write the word equation for respiration.
What gas do plants take in?
What happens when we burn wood or coal?

teach.heading: Carbon is everywhere
bullets: In the air as carbon dioxide
teach.note: Carbon is essential for life; all living things contain carbon compounds. Carbon dioxide makes up about 0.04% of the air.

teach.heading: Photosynthesis removes CO₂
teach.note: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (light energy needed). Plants are the main way carbon enters living things.

teach.heading: Feeding and respiration
bullets: Respiration returns CO₂ to the air
teach.note: All living things, including plants, respire and release CO₂. Decomposers also release CO₂ when they break down dead matter.

teach.heading: Combustion and fossil fuels
bullets: Fossil fuels formed from dead organisms
Adds CO₂ quickly to the air
teach.note: Coal, oil, gas formed over millions of years. Burning them releases CO₂ stored for millions of years in a much shorter time. Link to climate change next lessons.

teach.heading: Model the cycle
teach.note: Pupils draw the cycle with boxes (air, plants, animals, fossil fuels, decomposers) and arrows labelled photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, combustion, decay. Safe at-home demo: breathe out onto a cold surface to see water vapour.

practice: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the air?
Name two processes that return CO₂ to the air.
Why are fossil fuels a store of carbon?
independent: Draw and label a carbon cycle diagram with at least six labelled arrows.
Explain how carbon atoms in a carbon dioxide molecule can end up in a cow.
Write a paragraph explaining how burning fossil fuels changes the carbon cycle.
exit: Name two processes in the carbon cycle.
What does photosynthesis do to carbon dioxide?
lessons.homework: Trace the journey of a carbon atom from the air to your body and back again, in a comic strip.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a partly completed diagram. Stretch: compare time scales for combustion and fossil fuel formation.

lessons.title: Compounds and chemical formulae
objectives: Define a compound and explain how it differs from a mixture
Write simple chemical formulae and names of compounds
Explain how properties of a compound differ from its elements

keywords.def: a substance made of two or more elements chemically joined
symbols and numbers showing the atoms in a compound
the attraction that holds atoms together
a substance that takes part in a chemical reaction

starter: Bismillah. Write the symbols for sodium and chlorine.
What is an element?
Is water an element or a compound? Why?

teach.heading: Compounds
teach.note: Water, carbon dioxide, salt, sugar. Compounds can only be separated by chemical reactions.

teach.heading: Formulae
teach.note: The small number refers to the atom before it. Practise: MgO, CaCO₃ (1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O), H₂SO₄ (2 H, 1 S, 4 O).

teach.heading: Naming compounds
teach.note: Rule: a metal + non-metal compound ends in -ide. Compounds containing oxygen and another element often end in -ate. Do not push beyond basic.

teach.heading: New properties
teach.note: Practical demonstration safe online: show a video of iron and sulfur heated to form iron sulfide and the magnet test. Do not attempt at home. Sodium (explosive in water) and chlorine (poisonous gas) form table salt which is safe to eat.

teach.heading: Compounds vs mixtures
teach.note: Compare iron and sulfur mixed (magnet separates them) with iron sulfide. Misconception: mixing always forms a compound.

practice: How many atoms of each element are in H₂SO₄?
Name the compound formed when magnesium reacts with oxygen.
Why is table salt safe even though sodium and chlorine are dangerous?
independent: Complete a table of formula, elements, atoms of each and name for six compounds.
Write a paragraph comparing a compound and a mixture, using iron and sulfur as an example.
Draw particle diagrams of an element, a compound and a mixture.
exit: What is the formula of carbon dioxide?
What type of change makes a compound?
lessons.homework: Find the formula for five compounds around your home (e.g. on food or cleaning labels) and say what elements they contain.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide models with coloured circles for atoms. Stretch: explain the formula of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.

lessons.title: Energy requirements
objectives: Explain why different people need different amounts of energy
Estimate daily basal energy requirements
Use data to compare the energy needs of different people

keywords.def: the energy the body needs at rest each day
the amount of energy a person needs each day
how much physical movement a person does
a unit of energy; 1 kJ = 1000 joules

starter: Bismillah. Name two foods with a high energy content.
Does a footballer need the same energy as an office worker? Why?
What is energy measured in?

teach.heading: Energy at rest
bullets: The body uses energy even at rest
teach.note: BMR is the energy needed for basic life processes. A rough estimate is about 4.2 kJ per kilogram of body mass per hour. This is an approximation; formulae used by dietitians are more complex.

teach.heading: Estimating BMR
teach.note: Work through the example step by step. Remind pupils this is an estimate. Real needs are higher once activity is included.

teach.heading: Factors affecting needs
teach.note: Teenagers need more energy for growth. Compare a 14-year-old athlete with a sedentary adult. Avoid comparing students' bodies; use anonymous cases.

teach.heading: Matching energy in and out
teach.note: Keep a gentle tone. Discuss that growth, health and happiness matter more than any number. Refer worried pupils to a trusted adult.

teach.heading: Fasting and energy
bullets: Eat balanced meals at suhoor and iftar
teach.note: Briefly connect to Ramadan eating habits for older Muslims. Starchy wholegrain foods release energy slowly. Keep optional and respectful.

practice: Estimate the BMR of a 45 kg person using 4.2 × mass × 24.
Why does a swimmer need more energy than a person sitting in an office?
Name two factors that affect energy requirements.
independent: Calculate the BMR of people with masses 40 kg, 55 kg and 70 kg.
Draw a bar chart comparing the energy needs of three people with different activity levels (data supplied).
Write an explanation of why energy needs differ.
exit: What is BMR?
State one reason why a teenager needs more energy.
lessons.homework: Work out your approximate BMR with your own mass in kg and explain what the number means.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a worked example to copy. Stretch: explain why this estimate is only rough.

lessons.title: Mixtures and dissolving
objectives: Define mixture, solute, solvent and solution
Explain that dissolving is not disappearing
Describe factors affecting how much solute dissolves

keywords.def: two or more substances that are not chemically joined
a substance that dissolves in a solvent
a liquid in which a solute dissolves
how much of a solute can dissolve in a given amount of solvent

starter: Bismillah. What is a compound?
What happens when you stir sugar into tea?
Give an example of a mixture.

teach.heading: Mixtures
teach.note: Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen. Properties of the mixture reflect its parts.

teach.heading: Solutions
teach.note: A solution is a mixture that is clear and uniform. Misconception: dissolved sugar has disappeared. Mass is conserved: weigh the sugar and water before and after.

teach.heading: Mass is conserved
bullets: Evaporate the water to get the solute back
teach.note: Safe at-home demo using a kitchen scale: mass of cup of water plus sugar before and after stirring. Evaporate a salt solution on a saucer on a sunny windowsill.

teach.heading: Factors affecting solubility
bullets: A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more
teach.note: Most solids are more soluble in hot water. Gases are less soluble in warmer water. Use warm tap water only; no boiling water.

teach.heading: Investigating solubility
bullets: Add salt one spoon at a time
Count spoonfuls until no more dissolves
teach.note: Safe practical: cold and warm tap water, salt or sugar, a teaspoon. Record spoonfuls dissolved. Control variables: volume of water, stirring, spoon size.

practice: Identify the solute and solvent in salty water.
A student weighs 100 g of water and 10 g of salt. What is the mass of the solution?
What does saturated mean?
independent: Draw particle diagrams of a solid solute, a solvent, and the resulting solution.
Record the results of the solubility test and write a conclusion.
Explain why dissolving is a physical change.
exit: Define solvent and solute.
Why has the sugar not disappeared when it dissolves?
lessons.homework: Predict and test whether sugar or salt dissolves more in the same amount of warm water. Explain the results.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a frame to label solute, solvent and solution. Stretch: explain why gases are less soluble in hot water.

lessons.title: The atmosphere and the greenhouse effect
objectives: Describe the composition of the Earth's atmosphere
Explain the greenhouse effect
Describe how human activity increases carbon dioxide levels

keywords.def: the layer of gases surrounding the Earth
a gas such as carbon dioxide or methane that traps heat
the trapping of heat by gases in the atmosphere
the average weather in a region over many years

starter: Bismillah. Name two gases in the air.
What is the difference between weather and climate?
What process removes CO₂ from the air?

teach.heading: Atmosphere
teach.note: Also argon (about 1%) and water vapour. Draw a pie chart. Carbon dioxide is a trace gas but has a big effect.

teach.heading: Greenhouse effect
bullets: The Earth gives out infrared radiation
Greenhouse gases trap some of it
teach.note: The greenhouse effect is natural and necessary: without it, Earth's average temperature would be about -18 degrees Celsius instead of about 15. Misconception: the greenhouse effect is the same as the ozone hole.

teach.heading: Greenhouse gases
teach.note: Methane comes from livestock and rice paddies and gas leaks. Water vapour amplifies warming but its level depends on temperature.

teach.heading: Rising carbon dioxide
bullets: About 280 ppm before the industrial era
teach.note: Keep to scientific facts; measurements from the Mauna Loa Observatory since 1958 and ice cores show the rise. Quote as approximate.

teach.heading: Model the greenhouse effect
bullets: Two jars, one with a lid
teach.note: Safe at-home practical: two clear jars or bottles with thermometers, one with cling film. Place in sun for 30 minutes. Never leave in direct hot sun for long. Note that the model shows trapped warm air, which is not exactly the same mechanism.

practice: What percentage of the air is oxygen?
Name two greenhouse gases.
Why is the greenhouse effect necessary for life on Earth?
independent: Draw a pie chart of the atmosphere's composition.
Draw a labelled diagram of the greenhouse effect.
Explain how burning fossil fuels increases the greenhouse effect.
exit: Name one greenhouse gas.
How do human activities add to the greenhouse effect?
lessons.homework: Make a flowchart showing how burning fuel leads to a warmer atmosphere.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a diagram template and a word bank. Stretch: distinguish the natural from the enhanced greenhouse effect.

lessons.title: The digestive system
objectives: Name the organs of the digestive system and their functions
Describe the journey of food through the gut
Explain the role of enzymes in digestion

keywords.def: breaking down large food molecules into small soluble ones
a biological catalyst that speeds up reactions
the tube from mouth to stomach
movement of digested food into the blood

starter: Bismillah. Why must food be digested?
Name the nutrient groups.
Where do you think digestion starts?

teach.heading: Why digest?
bullets: They cannot pass into the blood
Digestion makes them small and soluble
teach.note: Starch to glucose, protein to amino acids, fats to fatty acids and glycerol. Analogy: break a long chain into links.

teach.heading: The gut
teach.note: Peristalsis: waves of muscle contraction push food. Stomach acid (hydrochloric acid, pH about 2) kills bacteria and helps protease enzymes work.

teach.heading: Intestines
teach.note: Egestion is removing undigested food. Do not confuse with excretion (waste from metabolism). Liver makes bile; pancreas makes enzymes.

teach.heading: Enzymes
teach.note: Enzymes are specific. Amylase is in saliva and the pancreas. Put a cracker in your mouth and chew for a minute; it tastes sweeter as starch becomes sugar. Safe if no allergies.

teach.heading: Model the gut
bullets: Banana in a bag for the stomach
teach.note: Safe at-home model with a zip bag, banana or bread, juice and a clean tights leg. Not to be eaten after. Wash hands afterwards.

practice: What does amylase break down?
Where does most absorption take place?
Put the parts of the gut in order from mouth to anus.
independent: Draw the digestive system with labels and functions.
Complete a table for enzyme, substrate, product.
Explain why digestion must happen before nutrients enter the blood.
exit: What is an enzyme?
Name the organ where most digestion is completed.
lessons.homework: Write a story called 'The journey of a sandwich', mentioning each organ and its function.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a gut diagram and cards of functions to match. Stretch: explain why the stomach does not digest itself (mucus lining).

lessons.title: Separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation and chromatography
objectives: Choose a suitable method to separate a mixture
Describe filtration, evaporation and chromatography
Interpret a chromatogram

keywords.def: separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper
the solid left on the filter paper
the liquid that passes through the filter paper
separating substances by how far they travel on paper

starter: Bismillah. What is a mixture?
How would you get sand out of water?
How would you get salt out of salt water?

teach.heading: Choosing a method
teach.note: Introduce methods: sieving, magnet, filtration, evaporation, crystallisation, chromatography, distillation. Ask which method for each mixture.

teach.heading: Filtration
teach.note: Sand and water. The filter paper has tiny holes. Particles of dissolved substances are too small to be trapped, so salt passes through.

teach.heading: Evaporation
teach.note: Rock salt: grind, dissolve in water, filter to remove sand, evaporate to get salt. Safe at home: leave salt solution on a saucer in the sun for several days instead of heating.

teach.heading: Chromatography
teach.note: Safe at-home practical: washable felt pen dot on a coffee filter strip, with the tip dipping in water in a glass. Different colours separate. Use pencil for the start line, never pen.

teach.heading: Reading a chromatogram
teach.note: Forensic uses; testing food colourings. Rf value (distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent) is a GCSE idea but could be an extension.

practice: Which method separates sand from water?
How could you get pure water from salt water?
A chromatogram shows three spots. Is the ink pure?
independent: Write a method to separate a mixture of sand, salt and iron filings.
Carry out the chromatography of a felt pen and describe the results.
Complete a table listing the mixture, method and reason for choosing it.
exit: What is the residue?
What does chromatography show about a coloured ink?
lessons.homework: Plan how to separate a mixture of rice, salt and iron filings and justify each step.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a flow chart with missing words. Stretch: calculate Rf values for given distances.

lessons.title: The small intestine, villi and gut bacteria
objectives: Explain how the small intestine is adapted for absorption
Describe the role of villi and capillaries
Describe the importance of bacteria in the gut

keywords.def: tiny finger-like projections lining the small intestine
movement of digested food into the blood
the total area available for exchange
microorganisms living in the intestines that help digestion

starter: Bismillah. What is the function of the small intestine?
Define digestion.
Why does a larger surface area help diffusion?

teach.heading: Absorption
bullets: Digested food passes into the blood
This happens in the small intestine
teach.note: Link to diffusion from Year 7. The concentration of digested food is higher in the gut than in the blood.

teach.heading: Villi
teach.note: One cell thick for short diffusion distance; capillaries take away the absorbed food so the concentration gradient stays steep. The lining has a surface area of about the size of a tennis court (commonly quoted, treat as approximate).

teach.heading: Adaptations
teach.note: Ask pupils to link each adaptation to faster absorption. Use a model such as a towel (surface area) compared to a flat sheet.

teach.heading: Gut bacteria
bullets: Trillions live in the large intestine
teach.note: Bacteria such as Lactobacillus are helpful; most are harmless. Antibiotics can disturb them. Yoghurt contains live bacteria.

teach.heading: Looking after your gut
teach.note: Cleanliness is half of faith (hadith in Sahih Muslim); washing hands before meals prevents infection. Safe at-home model: compare a flat paper towel with a crumpled one for surface area absorption of coloured water.

practice: What are villi?
Explain why villi have a rich blood supply.
Name one job of gut bacteria.
independent: Draw and label a villus with capillaries and thin wall.
Explain three adaptations of the small intestine for absorption.
Compare absorbing water with a flat towel and a folded towel and relate to villi.
exit: What do villi do?
Why do villi have thin walls?
lessons.homework: Make a model of a villus from craft materials and label its adaptations.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled villus to colour. Stretch: explain why the concentration gradient must be maintained.

lessons.title: Climate change: effects and responses
objectives: Describe evidence for climate change
Explain possible effects of global warming
Evaluate ways to reduce carbon dioxide emissions

keywords.def: the rise in the Earth's average temperature
long-term changes in temperature and weather patterns
the total greenhouse gases produced by a person or activity
energy from sources that will not run out, such as wind and solar

starter: Bismillah. Name a greenhouse gas.
How does burning fossil fuels affect the atmosphere?
What is the difference between weather and climate?

teach.heading: Evidence for warming
teach.note: Global average temperature has risen by around 1.1 to 1.2 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s. Use graphs of data. Distinguish weather (one cold day) from climate (long-term average).

teach.heading: Possible effects
teach.note: Discuss effects on people in different countries, including those already facing floods and drought. Compassion for others (rahma). Avoid frightening predictions; stay with evidence.

teach.heading: Reducing emissions
teach.note: Solar, wind, hydroelectric. Energy efficiency (LED bulbs). Planting trees removes CO₂ through photosynthesis but cannot solve the problem alone.

teach.heading: Personal choices
teach.note: Link to Islamic ethics: avoid waste, be a good steward of the Earth. Discuss collective action as well as individual action.

teach.heading: Evaluating solutions
teach.note: Pupils evaluate two solutions with reasons. Teach a balanced argument structure: 'One advantage is ... However ...'.

practice: Give one piece of evidence for global warming.
Name two ways to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.
Why does planting trees help?
independent: Plot a line graph of the data given (global temperature by decade) and describe the trend.
Write a balanced paragraph about the advantages and disadvantages of wind power.
Create an action plan with three things your family can do to reduce its carbon footprint.
exit: Define carbon footprint.
State one effect of global warming.
lessons.homework: Calculate and record one week's electricity or car use at home and suggest three savings.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide pre-labelled axes for the graph. Stretch: evaluate whether individuals or governments are more able to change emissions.

lessons.title: Distillation and purity
objectives: Describe simple and fractional distillation
Explain why distillation works using boiling points
Use melting and boiling points to test purity

keywords.def: separating liquids by evaporating then condensing them
separating a mixture of liquids with different boiling points
contains only one substance
a tube that cools vapour so it turns back into liquid

starter: Bismillah. Name three separation techniques.
What is the boiling point of water?
What is condensation?

teach.heading: Simple distillation
bullets: Water boils and turns to vapour
teach.note: Salt has a much higher boiling point so stays behind. The distillate is pure water. Used to obtain drinking water from the sea in many countries.

teach.heading: Fractional distillation
bullets: Separates liquids with different boiling points
The lowest boiling point comes off first
Used for crude oil and ethanol
teach.note: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C. The fractionating column gives repeated evaporation and condensation. In industry, crude oil is separated into petrol, diesel etc. Keep alcohol context minimal; use crude oil as the main example.

teach.heading: Pure substances
teach.note: Chemists mean something different from everyday 'pure' (e.g. pure orange juice is a mixture). Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point.

teach.heading: Solar still
bullets: Cling film cover with a weight
teach.note: Safe at-home practical: salt water in a large bowl, empty cup in the middle, cling film over the top with a small weight over the cup. Place in sunlight; water condenses and drips into the cup. Taste is not tested.

teach.heading: Water from the sea
teach.note: Link to countries in the Gulf that depend on desalination. Discuss costs and the importance of not wasting water.

practice: Why does salt stay behind in the flask during distillation?
Which liquid comes off first in fractional distillation: ethanol or water?
A solid melts between 120 and 125 °C. Is it pure?
independent: Draw and label the apparatus for simple distillation.
Explain how fractional distillation works using the idea of boiling points.
Evaluate the use of desalination for providing drinking water.
exit: What is a pure substance?
What does the condenser do?
lessons.homework: Write a short report on how seawater can be turned into drinking water.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled apparatus diagram. Stretch: explain why the fractionating column is cooler at the top.
